intro: The terminal is where Claude Code does a lot of its work. Learn to read what it's typing.

1.summary: Terminal vs shell, how a command is built, and the core navigation commands.

lesson.title: The terminal: texting your computer
lesson.body:
The **terminal** is an app window where you control your computer by typing instead of clicking. On a Mac it's called Terminal (or iTerm, or the panel inside VS Code).

Inside it runs a **shell**, the program that reads what you type and carries it out. The Mac's default shell is **zsh**; another common one is **bash**. That's why Claude Code's terminal tool is called "Bash."

The **prompt** is the little bit of text (often ending in `%` or `$`) that means "ready, type something." Everything you type after it is a **command**.
lesson.pm: The terminal isn't more powerful because it's mysterious. It's powerful because commands can be saved, repeated and automated, which is exactly why AI agents love it.

lesson.title: Anatomy of a command
lesson.body:
Most commands follow the same shape:

```
ls -la ~/Dev
```

- `ls` is the **command** (the verb): list files.
- `-la` are **flags** (options): `l` = long details, `a` = include hidden files.
- `~/Dev` is the **argument**: what to act on.

The five you'll see most:

- `pwd`: print working directory ("where am I?")
- `ls`: list what's in this folder
- `cd folder`: change directory (move into a folder)
- `mkdir name`: make a new folder
- `cat file`: print a file's contents
lesson.pm: Once you can split a command into verb, options and target, you can read almost any command Claude Code runs, even ones you've never seen.

cards.back: An app window where you control the computer by typing commands.
The program inside the terminal that reads and runs your commands. zsh and bash are common ones.
Print working directory: shows which folder you're in.
Lists the files and folders in the current folder.
Change directory: moves you into another folder, e.g. `cd src`.
An option added to a command, usually starting with `-` or `--`, e.g. `ls -la` or `npm install --save`.

quiz.why: Options starting with a dash are flags. `~/Dev` is the argument.

quiz.q: Which command shows the folder you're currently in?
quiz.why: pwd = print working directory. ls lists, cd moves, cat prints a file.

quiz.q: What's the difference between the terminal and the shell?
options: Terminal is the window; shell runs commands
Terminal runs commands; shell is the window
Terminal is for Macs; shell is for Windows
They're two names for the same program
quiz.why: The terminal is the app window. The shell (zsh, bash) reads and runs what you type.
`cat` prints a file's contents to the screen.
zsh is the Mac's default shell; bash is another common one.

2.summary: grep, pipes, chaining, installs, and the commands that deserve respect.

lesson.title: Searching and chaining: grep, | and &&
lesson.body:
**grep** searches inside files for text:

```
grep -rn "TODO" src/
```

That means: search for TODO, `-r` recursively (in every subfolder), `-n` showing line numbers, inside src/.

A **pipe** `|` sends one command's output into the next, like an assembly line:

```
grep -rn "TODO" src/ | wc -l
```

This finds every TODO, then `wc -l` counts the lines, so you get the number of TODOs.

`&&` means "then, but only if the first one worked": `npm install && npm run build`.
lesson.pm: Pipes are why the terminal is so good for quick questions like "how many TODOs are in this codebase?" You can ask Claude Code exactly these kinds of questions.

lesson.title: Commands to respect
lesson.body:
Some commands deserve a second look before you approve them:

- `rm` deletes files **permanently**. There's no Trash. `rm -rf folder` deletes a whole folder and everything inside, without asking.
- `sudo` runs a command as the computer's administrator.
- `npm install` / `pip install` download outside code packages from the internet.
- `git push --force` overwrites shared history.

Useful ones to know:

- **Ctrl+C** stops whatever is running.
- **Environment variables** are named settings the shell passes to programs, like `$HOME` or `API_KEY`. `export NAME=value` sets one.
lesson.pm: When Claude Code asks permission for a Bash command, reading it (verb, flags, target) is your safety check. Anything with `rm -rf`, `sudo` or `--force` deserves a pause.

cards.back: Searches inside files for text. `-r` = search all subfolders, `-n` = show line numbers.
Sends one command's output into the next command, like an assembly line.
Runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded.
Permanently deletes a folder and everything in it, without asking. No Trash.
Runs a command with administrator powers. Use with care.
A named setting (like `$HOME` or `API_KEY`) the shell passes to programs.
Stops the command that's currently running in the terminal.

options: A count of lines containing TODO
A list of files named TODO
A new file listing all TODOs
quiz.why: grep finds matching lines, the pipe passes them on, `wc -l` counts them.

quiz.q: In `npm install && npm run build`, when does the build run?
options: At the same time as the install
Whether or not the install works
quiz.why: `&&` runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded.

options: Permanently delete dist and its contents
Move dist and its contents to the Trash
Rename dist to a backup folder
quiz.why: rm deletes with no Trash; -r includes everything inside; -f skips confirmation.

quiz.q: Which keys stop a command that's running in the terminal?

options: Runs a command with admin powers
Runs a command in the background
Runs a command on a remote server
Runs a command without any output
quiz.why: sudo = run as the administrator ("superuser"). Worth a pause before approving.
